title: Act II, Scene III
focus: Friar Laurence agrees to marry them

teacherSummary.text: At dawn Friar Laurence gathers herbs and reflects that every plant can heal or poison. Romeo arrives and asks him to marry him to Juliet. The Friar scolds his fickleness about Rosaline but agrees, hoping the marriage will end the feud.

Two such opposed kings encamp them still
In man as well as herbs, grace and rude will;
And where the worser is predominant,
Full soon the canker death eats up that plant.
Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast.

words.sentence:
But come, young waverer, come, go with me,
In one respect I’ll thy assistant be;
For this alliance may so happy prove,
To turn your households’ rancour to pure love.

Be plain, good son, and homely in thy drift;
Riddling confession finds but riddling shrift.

I have been feasting with mine enemy,
Where on a sudden one hath wounded me,
That’s by me wounded: both our remedies
Within thy help and holy physic lies:
I bear no hatred, blessed man, for, lo,
My intercession likewise steads my foe.

segments.script: Friars were members of mendicant religious orders; Franciscans were known for herb lore and practical care. Secret marriages were legal but irregular in canon law. The Friar's speech on plants foreshadows the potion; his political hope explains his risky help. Characterization: Friar Laurence, gathering herbs, reflects that everything can heal or harm depending on use. Foreshadowing: His knowledge of plants ("Poison hath residence and medicine power") prepares the potion. Irony: He scolds Romeo's fickleness yet agrees to marry him, hoping to end the feud. Watch for light and dark: The lovers describe each other as light in darkness (torches, sun, stars, lightning), yet they can meet only at night, and daylight brings danger. In this scene: “The grey-eyed morn smiles on the frowning night, / Chequering the eastern clouds with streaks of light, / And flecked darkness” (Act II, Scene III, Friar Laurence).

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “young men’s love then lies / Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes” slowly and put it in my own words: The Friar says young men's love lies not in their hearts but in their eyes. Next, craft. I notice the rhyming couplet, a neat moral that sounds like a proverb. The strongest word is “eyes”: it suggests love based on looks. Then, effect. What is Friar Laurence teasing Romeo about? My answer: The Friar doubts Romeo's sudden change from Rosaline to Juliet; he agrees to marry them hoping to end the feud, a risky choice.
